title: How to Get An Adult ADHD Diagnosis in Canada
body_markdown:
If you've been wondering whether you might have ADHD, you're not alone. Adult ADHD diagnoses have been rising sharply in Canada over the last decade, particularly among women and adults who went undiagnosed as kids.


The problem is that getting diagnosed in Canada can be genuinely confusing. The public system is slow, with waits for a psychiatric assessment stretching anywhere from six months to over two years depending on your province and city. The private system is faster but often cash-pay. Family doctors can sometimes help but many don't feel comfortable diagnosing ADHD. And on top of that, there's a growing landscape of virtual clinics with wildly different models.


We hear it constantly from our Canadian community: *where do I even start, and what's actually worth paying for?*


This guide walks through what a quality ADHD assessment looks like, how the Canadian system actually works, your public and private options, and how to find a practitioner you can trust.


## Why finding the right practitioner matters


Not all ADHD assessments are created equal. Some assessments may be brief, while others take hours, use validated clinical instruments, factor in your full history, and look for other things that can look like ADHD but aren't (anxiety, trauma, sleep issues, thyroid conditions, and more).


A rushed diagnosis can mean:


- Missing a co-occurring condition that needs its own treatment
- Being given a prescription that isn't right for you
- Getting labelled with something that doesn't actually fit
- Paying out of pocket for an assessment that won't be accepted for workplace or school accommodations


A thorough diagnosis gives you a foundation you can build on. It's worth taking the time to get it right.


## What a good ADHD assessment looks like


A quality adult ADHD assessment usually includes:


- **A detailed clinical interview** , typically 45-60 minutes for the first visit, where a licensed practitioner walks through your current symptoms and childhood history
- **Validated screening instruments** , such as the ASRS, CAARS, DIVA-5, or the WURS for retrospective childhood symptoms. The Canadian ADHD Practice Guidelines (published by CADDRA) recommend using validated tools alongside clinical judgement
- **Differential diagnosis** , meaning the practitioner actively considers whether something else might be going on (anxiety, depression,[autism (AuDHD)](https://www.shimmer.care/blog/audhd-autism-adhd-comorbidity) , trauma, sleep disorders, thyroid issues)
- **Collateral information when relevant** , like input from a partner, family member, or old school records that help confirm childhood onset
- **A real treatment plan** , not just a prescription. Something that discusses prescriptions, behavioral support, lifestyle changes, and follow-up cadence


## How to find an adult ADHD assessment practitioner in Canada


There are more options than most people realize, and the right one depends on your province, your timeline, your budget, and your insurance.


**Public system (covered by your province):**


- **Your family doctor (GP).** Family physicians across Canada can diagnose and prescribe for adult ADHD, though not all feel comfortable doing so. If you have a family doctor, this is often the first (and cheapest) place to start. If they're not comfortable managing ADHD, they can refer you to a psychiatrist
- **Psychiatrist referral through your GP.** Required in most provinces. Covered by your provincial plan (OHIP, MSP, Alberta Health, etc.), but wait times are long. ADHD-specialized psychiatrists in major Canadian cities often have 1-2+ year waits
- **University or community mental health clinics.** Some have adult ADHD programs, often with wait lists but no out-of-pocket cost
- **Provincially-funded virtual care** where available.


**Private system (out of pocket, often reimbursable via extended health benefits):**


- **Private virtual ADHD clinics.** A growing category offering virtual assessment and ongoing care. Typically nurse-practitioner-led, with faster access and clearer pricing.
- **Private psychiatrists.** Rare in Canada (most are in the public system), but a few operate privately.
- **Psychologists for assessment.** Psychologists can diagnose ADHD and often administer more comprehensive psychoeducational assessments, but cannot write prescriptions (except in specific provincial carve-outs). Useful if you need documentation for workplace or school accommodations. Costs typically run $1,500-$3,500 for a full battery


Whichever route you take, the quality signals above are what to look for: a thorough first visit, validated instruments, differential diagnosis, and a real plan for ongoing care.


### Questions worth asking any ADHD practitioner


Two questions that cut through most of the noise, from an often-cited CHADD piece by Dr. Oren W. Mason:


1. **How many patients with ADHD do you currently treat?** A good rule of thumb is an active ADHD panel of 50-100+. Enough that the practitioner is seeing the full range of presentations and keeping up with the research
2. **Do you (or your practice) like treating ADHD?** Not every mental health practitioner enjoys ADHD care. The answer tells you whether you're walking into a practice that's genuinely interested, or one that treats it as an afterthought


A few practical things worth checking before you book:


- Average wait time for a first evaluation
- Cost structure, and whether they bill directly to your extended health benefits
- Standard follow-up cadence (ongoing ADHD care usually means 2-12 visits per year)
- Whether the practice offers or refers to ancillary services like therapy, ADHD coaching, or educational specialists
- Whether they can prescribe controlled substances (stimulants). Important: nurse practitioners in Canada can prescribe stimulants in all provinces


That last point about ancillary services matters more than people realize. The strongest ADHD care is multimodal. Practices that acknowledge this, either by offering those services themselves or by actively referring to specialists in them, tend to deliver better outcomes.


*Source: Mason, O.W.,*["Where Can Adults with ADHD Find the Best Treatment?"](https://chadd.org/adhd-news/adhd-news-adults/where-can-adults-with-adhd-find-the-best-treatment-2/) *CHADD Attention Magazine, October 2019.*

## What to expect from The Maple Beyond ADHD program


Here's a look at the Beyond ADHD experience:


- **Free self-assessment:** Before you pay anything, Beyond ADHD uses a clinically validated questionnaire to determine if ADHD care is the right next step or if another underlying condition should be treated first.
- **Practitioner assessment:** Once it's determined that ADHD care may be the right next step, you book the ADHD assessment with a practitioner. Prior to meeting with the practitioner, you complete a long-form assessment questionnaire with validated instruments like the CAARS (ADHD rating scale), GAD-7 (anxiety) and PHQ-9 (depression) to flag co-occurring conditions


- In preparation for your next visit, the practitioner reviews your intake and you may be asked to gather additional information.


- **Diagnosis and treatment plan:** Your practitioner walks through the diagnostic conclusion and, if ADHD is the diagnosis, discusses prescription options, non-prescription supports and the plan going forward
- **Follow-up care:** Ongoing prescription management, side effect monitoring and treatment adjustments. Visit cadence spaces out once your treatment is stable


## How to prepare for your ADHD assessment


Showing up prepared makes a real difference, especially since many first visits are only 30-60 minutes. The more concrete you can be about your experience, the better your practitioner can assess what's going on. A few things worth doing before your visit:


- **Write out your symptoms with specific examples.** Not just "I have trouble focusing" but "I regularly start three projects at work and finish none of them by the deadline" or "I lose my keys multiple times a week." Concrete examples anchor an assessment far better than general descriptions
- **Pull evidence of childhood symptoms.** ADHD is a developmental condition, which means symptoms have to have been present in childhood (even if they weren't recognized). Old report cards, memories of school struggles, or a conversation with a parent or older sibling can all help. Common childhood signals: being called "smart but not applying yourself," struggling to finish homework, chronic lateness, forgetting assignments, trouble sitting still, daydreaming
- **Think about family history.** ADHD has a strong genetic component. Any family members with diagnosed ADHD, learning differences, anxiety, depression, or substance use issues are worth noting
- **List what you've already tried.** Previous prescriptions (ADHD or otherwise), therapy modalities, coaching, lifestyle changes, supplements, and productivity systems. What's worked, what hasn't, and what you're currently on
- **Bring your own questions.** Things like: What assessment instruments will you use? How do you decide between different prescriptions? What's your approach if a prescription isn't the right fit? How often will we meet after diagnosis? Can you refer me for therapy or coaching?


If you're a late-diagnosed adult, especially a woman or AFAB person, it's worth noting any patterns associated with less-recognized ADHD presentations: internalized symptoms (anxiety, perfectionism, people-pleasing), masking, chronic burnout, strong academic performance that collapsed in adulthood when structure disappeared. Practitioners who specialize in adult ADHD will recognize these patterns, but surfacing them explicitly helps.


## What happens after you get diagnosed


Getting the diagnosis is the beginning, not the end. The first six to twelve months after an adult ADHD diagnosis can be a lot, both practically and emotionally. Knowing what to expect helps.


**Finding the right prescription and dose.** If you start a prescription, expect a titration process. Your practitioner will typically start you on a low dose and adjust based on how you respond, side effects, and how long it lasts for you. This usually takes a few months of visits to dial in. It's normal for the first medication or dose to not be the right one. If you're on a stimulant, you'll also learn how it interacts with sleep, caffeine, food, and your menstrual cycle (if applicable). All worth tracking and bringing to appointments.


**Grief, relief, and anger are all common.** For late-diagnosed adults especially, a diagnosis often brings up a flood of feelings. Relief at finally having an explanation. Grief for the years spent struggling without one. Anger at teachers, parents, or systems that missed it. Reframing your whole life story through an ADHD lens takes time and is often harder than people expect. You got this.


**Treatment usually works best as a mix.** A prescription can be transformative for focus, impulse control, and energy regulation. It's often the fastest-acting piece. Alongside it, behavioural support (coaching, therapy, or both) helps you rebuild the systems, routines, and self-trust that got eroded over years of struggling. Research consistently shows that multimodal treatment produces better long-term outcomes than any one modality alone. Here's how the pieces fit together:


- **Prescriptions** address the neurochemistry: attention regulation, impulse control, executive function
- **Therapy** addresses the emotional: the anxiety, shame, trauma, or self-worth stuff that often shows up alongside ADHD, especially for late-diagnosed adults
- **ADHD coaching** addresses the practical: building systems, routines, and strategies that work with your ADHD brain. The place where insight turns into daily change


The three work differently and complement each other.


This is where coaching, therapy, and community become part of the picture.

## FAQs


**I think I might have ADHD but I'm not sure. Should I get assessed?**


If you've been wondering for a while, it's probably worth a conversation. A good assessment either confirms what you suspected or points you toward what else might be going on. Either outcome is useful.


**How long is the wait for an ADHD assessment in Canada?**


Through the public system, waits for a psychiatrist can range from 6 months to 2+ years depending on your province and city. In major cities, ADHD-specialized psychiatrists often have the longest waits. Private virtual clinics typically see patients within days to a couple of weeks.


**Can my family doctor diagnose and prescribe for ADHD?**


Yes, family physicians across Canada are legally able to diagnose adult ADHD and prescribe treatments. The practical reality is more mixed: some GPs are comfortable managing adult ADHD, others prefer to refer to a specialist. If your GP isn't comfortable, they can refer you to a psychiatrist or help you access a virtual clinic.


**Does OHIP (or my provincial plan) cover ADHD assessment?**


Visits with your family doctor and referrals to psychiatrists are covered by your provincial plan. Psychology assessments, private virtual clinics, and ongoing coaching or therapy generally are not. Private assessments and ongoing care are often reimbursable through extended health benefits, depending on your plan.


**How much does a private ADHD assessment cost in Canada?**


It depends on the provider. Beyond ADHD typically charges around $279 for a first assessment, $179 for a follow-up diagnosis visit, and about $99 for ongoing titration or management visits. Psychology-led psychoeducational assessments (useful for workplace or school accommodations) typically run $1,500-$3,500.


**Will my insurance cover a private ADHD assessment?**


Many Canadian extended health benefits plans will reimburse practitioner or psychologist visits under their mental health or paramedical categories. Coverage limits vary. Beyond ADHD has partnerships with health and student insurers, making it easier for people to access care. Check with your plan to see what's covered.


**Can I get an ADHD diagnosis online in Canada?**


Yes. Virtual clinics licensed in your province can legally diagnose adult ADHD, prescribe treatment, and manage ongoing care, provided their clinicians (whether NPs, physicians, or psychiatrists) are properly licensed. Virtual clinics cannot administer full psychoeducational batteries (those require in-person testing with a psychologist), so if you need that level of documentation for workplace or school accommodations, you'll want to see a psychologist in person.


**Does Shimmer coaching require a diagnosis?**


No. Our coaching is subclinical and works for anyone with ADHD traits, whether you're formally diagnosed, self-identifying, or still figuring it out.
